findings.title: Instance __dict__ ordering not guaranteed on PyPy
findings.description: Accessing __dict__ on an instance. In CPython 3.7+, instance dictionaries are insertion-ordered. In PyPy, instance dicts use hidden classes for performance — if __init__ adds attributes in different orders across calls, dict order is not guaranteed to match CPython's.
findings.suggestion: Do not rely on instance __dict__ ordering. If you need ordered attributes, define them explicitly in __init__ in a consistent order, or use __slots__ to make the layout fixed.

findings.title: __slots__ memory savings differ on PyPy
findings.description: Class 'ABC' defines __slots__. On CPython, __slots__ prevents __dict__ creation and gives predictable memory savings. On PyPy, object layout uses hidden classes — __slots__ works correctly but memory savings differ from CPython. Do not rely on specific memory numbers from CPython when running on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: __slots__ is still correct and beneficial on PyPy — just measure memory usage independently on each runtime rather than assuming CPython numbers apply.

findings.title: match/case requires Python 3.10+
findings.description: Structural pattern matching (match/case) was introduced in Python 3.10 (PEP 634). On Python 3.9 and below this is a SyntaxError — the entire module fails to import.
findings.suggestion: Replace with if/elif chains for Python 3.9 compatibility, or add requires-python = '>=3.10' to your pyproject.toml.

findings.title: id() values not stable across GC cycles on PyPy
findings.description: id() returns the memory address on CPython — stable for the object's lifetime. On PyPy, the GC may move objects in memory, so id() can return different values for the same object across GC cycles. Using id() for caching, hashing, or identity tracking may silently produce wrong results on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: Use object identity with 'is' instead of comparing id() values. For caching, use weakref or dedicated identity maps rather than id()-based keys.

findings.title: hash() values may differ between CPython and PyPy
findings.description: hash() is called here. On CPython, hash(-1) returns -2 because -1 is reserved as an error indicator in C. PyPy matches this for integers, but hash values for certain custom objects or edge cases may differ between runtimes. Code that stores or compares hash values across sessions or runtimes may silently fail.
findings.suggestion: Never store hash values persistently or compare them across different Python runtimes. Hash values are implementation-specific and not guaranteed to be consistent between CPython and PyPy.

findings.title: Generator cleanup timing differs on PyPy
findings.description: Generator '_iter_indented_subactions' yields inside a try/with block. On CPython, if a generator is abandoned mid-execution, the finally/cleanup runs promptly via reference counting. On PyPy, the generator is GC'd later — finally blocks and context manager __exit__ may run much later or at unpredictable times, silently leaking resources.
findings.suggestion: Always fully exhaust generators or use explicit close(): gen.close(). Use try/finally in the caller to guarantee cleanup rather than relying on generator GC.

findings.title: open() without encoding= uses platform-dependent encoding before 3.15
findings.description: open() is called in text mode without an explicit encoding= argument. Before Python 3.15, the default encoding is the platform locale — UTF-8 on Linux/Mac but often CP1252 or Latin-1 on Windows. This silently causes encoding errors or data corruption when code runs on different platforms. Python 3.15 (PEP 686) makes UTF-8 the universal default.
findings.suggestion: Always specify encoding explicitly: open(file, encoding='utf-8') This works correctly on all Python versions and platforms.

findings.suggestion: Use a list and join at the end: parts = []; parts.append(s); result = ''.join(parts). This avoids repeated string concatenation.

findings.title: sys.settrace() disables JIT and is unreliable on PyPy
findings.description: sys.settrace() is called. On CPython, this installs a tracing function for debugging and profiling. On PyPy, sys.settrace() disables the JIT compiler entirely — causing 10-100x performance degradation — and some trace events may not fire correctly. Coverage tools and debuggers using settrace will silently give incomplete results on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: For profiling on PyPy, use vmprof instead of settrace-based profilers. For coverage, use coverage.py with PyPy-specific configuration. Avoid settrace in production code on PyPy.

findings.title: Exception variable cleanup timing differs on PyPy
findings.description: Exception variable 'exc' is used after the except handler exits. CPython explicitly clears exception variables at the end of an except handler to break reference cycles. Depending on exception-variable lifetime can therefore interact differently with PyPy's garbage collector.
findings.suggestion: If 'exc' must remain available after the except block, explicitly copy it to another variable inside the handler, for example: saved_exc = exc.

findings.title: id() values not stable across GC cycles on PyPy
findings.description: id() returns the memory address on CPython — stable for the object's lifetime. On PyPy, the GC may move objects in memory, so id() can return different values for the same object across GC cycles. Using id() for caching, hashing, or identity tracking may silently produce wrong results on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: Use object identity with 'is' instead of comparing id() values. For caching, use weakref or dedicated identity maps rather than id()-based keys.

findings.title: Instance __dict__ ordering not guaranteed on PyPy
findings.description: Accessing __dict__ on an instance. In CPython 3.7+, instance dictionaries are insertion-ordered. In PyPy, instance dicts use hidden classes for performance — if __init__ adds attributes in different orders across calls, dict order is not guaranteed to match CPython's.
findings.suggestion: Do not rely on instance __dict__ ordering. If you need ordered attributes, define them explicitly in __init__ in a consistent order, or use __slots__ to make the layout fixed.

findings.title: Unsynchronized module-level mutable state may be unsafe in free-threaded Python
findings.description: Module-level mutable variable '_extension_cache' is mutated from runtime function code without recognizable synchronization. In a CPython free-threaded build, code that relies on the GIL to coordinate compound or unsynchronized access to shared state can behave differently.

On PyPy, the GC may move objects in memory, so id() can return different values for the same object across GC cycles. Using id() for caching, hashing, or identity tracking may silently produce wrong results on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: Use object identity with 'is' instead of comparing id() values. For caching, use weakref or dedicated identity maps rather than id()-based keys.

findings.title: String concatenation in loop is O(n²) on PyPy
findings.description: String variable 'lineno' is concatenated with += inside a loop. Repeated string concatenation can have different performance characteristics on PyPy and may become O(n²) for large inputs.
findings.suggestion: Use a list and join at the end: parts = []; parts.append(s); result = ''.join(parts). This avoids repeated string concatenation.

findings.title: Instance __dict__ ordering not guaranteed on PyPy
findings.description: Accessing __dict__ on an instance. In CPython 3.7+, instance dictionaries are insertion-ordered. In PyPy, instance dicts use hidden classes for performance — if __init__ adds attributes in different orders across calls, dict order is not guaranteed to match CPython's.
findings.suggestion: Do not rely on instance __dict__ ordering. If you need ordered attributes, define them explicitly in __init__ in a consistent order, or use __slots__ to make the layout fixed.

findings.title: inspect.ismethod() returns different results on PyPy
findings.description: inspect.ismethod() behaves differently on PyPy. On CPython, built-in method wrappers like [].__add__ are not considered methods. On PyPy, they are normal method objects and ismethod() returns True. Code inspecting built-in types may silently produce wrong results on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: Use callable() instead of inspect.ismethod() for checking if something can be called. If you need to distinguish built-in from Python methods, test explicitly with inspect.isbuiltin().

findings.title: locals() semantics changed in Python 3.13 (PEP 667)
findings.description: locals() is called here. Before Python 3.13, modifying the dict returned by locals() had undefined behaviour — changes sometimes affected local variables. In Python 3.13 (PEP 667), locals() returns a snapshot and modifying it never affects actual local variables. Code relying on locals() mutation will silently break.
findings.suggestion: Do not modify the dict returned by locals(). Use explicit variable assignment instead. If you need dynamic variable access, use a regular dict.

findings.title: hash() values may differ between CPython and PyPy
findings.description: hash() is called here. On CPython, hash(-1) returns -2 because -1 is reserved as an error indicator in C. PyPy matches this for integers, but hash values for certain custom objects or edge cases may differ between runtimes. Code that stores or compares hash values across sessions or runtimes may silently fail.
findings.suggestion: Never store hash values persistently or compare them across different Python runtimes. Hash values are implementation-specific and not guaranteed to be consistent between CPython and PyPy.

findings.title: sys.settrace() disables JIT and is unreliable on PyPy
findings.description: sys.settrace() is called. On CPython, this installs a tracing function for debugging and profiling. On PyPy, sys.settrace() disables the JIT compiler entirely — causing 10-100x performance degradation — and some trace events may not fire correctly. Coverage tools and debuggers using settrace will silently give incomplete results on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: For profiling on PyPy, use vmprof instead of settrace-based profilers. For coverage, use coverage.py with PyPy-specific configuration. Avoid settrace in production code on PyPy.

findings.title: Unsynchronized module-level mutable state may be unsafe in free-threaded Python
findings.description: Module-level mutable variable 'OPTIONFLAGS_BY_NAME' is mutated from runtime function code without recognizable synchronization. In a CPython free-threaded build, code that relies on the GIL to coordinate compound or unsynchronized access to shared state can behave differently.
findings.suggestion: If this state is shared across threads, protect compound mutations and read-modify-write sequences with a lock, or use an appropriate thread-safe abstraction. Individual built-in list/dict/set operations should not be treated as a blanket guarantee of thread safety.

findings.title: Overriding built-in methods may behave differently on PyPy
findings.description: Class 'EnumDict' subclasses 'dict' and overrides '__setitem__'. On CPython, internal C-level calls to built-in methods may bypass Python overrides. On PyPy, the same calls may go through the Python override. This can cause silent behaviour differences between runtimes.
findings.suggestion: Test the overridden method explicitly on both CPython and PyPy. Consider using composition instead of inheritance from built-in types.

findings.title: Deleting module/class attributes is significantly slower on PyPy
findings.description: Attribute '__notes__' is being deleted. On PyPy, module and class dictionaries are optimised under the assumption that deleting attributes is rare. Frequent attribute deletion is significantly slower on PyPy than on CPython and will silently degrade performance in hot paths.
findings.suggestion: Avoid frequent attribute deletion in hot code paths. Set attributes to None instead of deleting them, or restructure code to avoid deletion entirely.

findings.title: Unsynchronized module-level mutable state may be unsafe in free-threaded Python
findings.description: Module-level mutable variable '_cache' is mutated from runtime function code without recognizable synchronization. In a CPython free-threaded build, code that relies on the GIL to coordinate compound or unsynchronized access to shared state can behave differently.
findings.suggestion: If this state is shared across threads, protect compound mutations and read-modify-write sequences with a lock, or use an appropriate thread-safe abstraction. Individual built-in list/dict/set operations should not be treated as a blanket guarantee of thread safety.

findings.title: Relying on __del__ for resource cleanup breaks on PyPy
findings.description: __del__ calls 'close()' for resource cleanup. On CPython, __del__ is called immediately when the object goes out of scope (reference counting). On PyPy, the GC is non-reference-counting — __del__ may be called much later or not at all, silently leaking file handles, sockets, or locks.
findings.suggestion: Use context managers (with statement) or try/finally blocks for guaranteed cleanup. Never rely on __del__ for correctness.

findings.title: Deleting module/class attributes is significantly slower on PyPy
findings.description: Attribute '_readline' is being deleted. On PyPy, module and class dictionaries are optimised under the assumption that deleting attributes is rare. Frequent attribute deletion is significantly slower on PyPy than on CPython and will silently degrade performance in hot paths.
findings.suggestion: Avoid frequent attribute deletion in hot code paths. Set attributes to None instead of deleting them, or restructure code to avoid deletion entirely.

findings.title: Exceptions in __del__ appear at unpredictable times on PyPy
findings.description: __del__ contains code that may raise exceptions. On CPython, exceptions in __del__ produce a warning to stderr immediately when the object is collected. On PyPy, the warning appears at an unpredictable time — possibly long after the object was collected — making debugging very difficult.
findings.suggestion: Wrap all __del__ body in try/except to prevent exceptions from escaping: try: self.cleanup() except Exception: pass. Better: use context managers instead of __del__.

findings.title: __slots__ may not prevent __dict__ on Python < 3.10
findings.description: Class 'Fraction' defines __slots__ but inherits from a non-trivial base class. If any ancestor class has __dict__, __slots__ will NOT prevent __dict__ creation on the subclass. This behaviour is consistent across versions but commonly misunderstood — and Python 3.10 added clearer documentation and warnings around this pattern.
findings.suggestion: Verify that all ancestor classes also define __slots__ if you need to prevent __dict__ creation. Use __slots__ = () on base classes that should not have instance dictionaries.

findings.title: hash() values may differ between CPython and PyPy
findings.description: hash() is called here. On CPython, hash(-1) returns -2 because -1 is reserved as an error indicator in C. PyPy matches this for integers, but hash values for certain custom objects or edge cases may differ between runtimes. Code that stores or compares hash values across sessions or runtimes may silently fail.
findings.suggestion: Never store hash values persistently or compare them across different Python runtimes. Hash values are implementation-specific and not guaranteed to be consistent between CPython and PyPy.

findings.title: decimal module uses different backend on PyPy
findings.description: The decimal module is imported. On CPython, decimal uses a fast C implementation. On PyPy, it uses a pure Python/RPython implementation which is slower and may have subtle differences in rounding behaviour and context handling in edge cases.
findings.suggestion: Test decimal-heavy code on PyPy explicitly. For high-precision financial calculations, verify rounding behaviour matches expectations on both CPython and PyPy with your specific data.

findings.title: __slots__ memory savings differ on PyPy
findings.description: Class 'Fraction' defines __slots__. On CPython, __slots__ prevents __dict__ creation and gives predictable memory savings. On PyPy, object layout uses hidden classes — __slots__ works correctly but memory savings differ from CPython. Do not rely on specific memory numbers from CPython when running on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: __slots__ is still correct and beneficial on PyPy — just measure memory usage independently on each runtime rather than assuming CPython numbers apply.

findings.title: int() no longer delegates to __trunc__() in Python 3.14
findings.description: __trunc__() method is defined here. Before Python 3.14, int() would call __trunc__() on objects that did not implement __int__() or __index__(). In Python 3.14, this delegation was removed — int(obj) now raises TypeError if __int__() and __index__() are missing, even if __trunc__() is defined. Custom numeric types relying on __trunc__() for int() conversion silently break on Python 3.14+.
findings.suggestion: Implement __int__() or __index__() instead of __trunc__(). def __int__(self): return int(self._value) __trunc__() is still called by math.trunc() but no longer by int().

findings.title: Instance __dict__ ordering not guaranteed on PyPy
findings.description: Accessing __dict__ on an instance. In CPython 3.7+, instance dictionaries are insertion-ordered. In PyPy, instance dicts use hidden classes for performance — if __init__ adds attributes in different orders across calls, dict order is not guaranteed to match CPython's.
findings.suggestion: Do not rely on instance __dict__ ordering. If you need ordered attributes, define them explicitly in __init__ in a consistent order, or use __slots__ to make the layout fixed.

findings.title: Generator cleanup timing differs on PyPy
findings.description: Generator '_iterdir' yields inside a try/with block. On CPython, if a generator is abandoned mid-execution, the finally/cleanup runs promptly via reference counting. On PyPy, the generator is GC'd later — finally blocks and context manager __exit__ may run much later or at unpredictable times, silently leaking resources.
findings.suggestion: Always fully exhaust generators or use explicit close(): gen.close(). Use try/finally in the caller to guarantee cleanup rather than relying on generator GC.

findings.title: File write without explicit flush may lose data on PyPy
findings.description: A file is opened for writing. On PyPy, file buffering behaviour differs from CPython — data may not be flushed to disk even after close() due to GC timing differences. Without explicit flush() or a context manager, writes can be silently lost on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: Always use 'with open(...) as f:' to guarantee flushing and closing. If not using a context manager, call f.flush() explicitly before f.close().

findings.title: id() values not stable across GC cycles on PyPy
findings.description: id() returns the memory address on CPython — stable for the object's lifetime. On PyPy, the GC may move objects in memory, so id() can return different values for the same object across GC cycles. Using id() for caching, hashing, or identity tracking may silently produce wrong results on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: Use object identity with 'is' instead of comparing id() values. For caching, use weakref or dedicated identity maps rather than id()-based keys.

findings.title: subprocess.PIPE buffering may cause deadlocks on PyPy
findings.description: Popen is called with stdin=PIPE. On PyPy, GC timing differences can cause subprocess pipe communication to deadlock or lose data silently — especially when both stdin and stdout use PIPE and the buffers fill up before communicate() is called.
findings.suggestion: Always use communicate() instead of read()/write() directly on pipes. communicate() handles buffering correctly on both CPython and PyPy.

findings.title: Exception variable cleanup timing differs on PyPy
findings.description: Exception variable 'val' is used after the except handler exits. CPython explicitly clears exception variables at the end of an except handler to break reference cycles. Depending on exception-variable lifetime can therefore interact differently with PyPy's garbage collector.
findings.suggestion: If 'val' must remain available after the except block, explicitly copy it to another variable inside the handler, for example: saved_exc = val.

findings.title: __debug__ is always True on PyPy — -O flag has no effect
findings.description: 'if __debug__:' block detected. On CPython, running with -O sets __debug__ to False, removing this code from execution. On PyPy, __debug__ is always True regardless of the -O flag — code inside 'if __debug__:' blocks always runs on PyPy, even when you expect it to be optimised away.
findings.suggestion: Do not rely on -O to remove debug code on PyPy. Use an explicit environment variable or config flag instead: DEBUG = os.getenv('DEBUG', '0') == '1'

findings.suggestion: Use object identity with 'is' instead of comparing id() values. For caching, use weakref or dedicated identity maps rather than id()-based keys.

findings.title: Generator cleanup timing differs on PyPy
findings.description: Generator '_replace_attribute' yields inside a try/with block. On CPython, if a generator is abandoned mid-execution, the finally/cleanup runs promptly via reference counting. On PyPy, the generator is GC'd later — finally blocks and context manager __exit__ may run much later or at unpredictable times, silently leaking resources.
findings.suggestion: Always fully exhaust generators or use explicit close(): gen.close(). Use try/finally in the caller to guarantee cleanup rather than relying on generator GC.

findings.title: Instance __dict__ ordering not guaranteed on PyPy
findings.description: Accessing __dict__ on an instance. In CPython 3.7+, instance dictionaries are insertion-ordered. In PyPy, instance dicts use hidden classes for performance — if __init__ adds attributes in different orders across calls, dict order is not guaranteed to match CPython's.
findings.suggestion: Do not rely on instance __dict__ ordering. If you need ordered attributes, define them explicitly in __init__ in a consistent order, or use __slots__ to make the layout fixed.

findings.title: __builtins__ is always a module on PyPy, never a dict
findings.description: __builtins__ is accessed here. On CPython, __builtins__ is the __builtin__ module in __main__ but a plain dict in other modules. On PyPy, __builtins__ is always the module — never a dict. Code checking isinstance(__builtins__, dict) or accessing __builtins__['name'] will silently fail on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: Use the builtins module directly instead: import builtins; builtins.print — this works consistently on both CPython and PyPy.

findings.title: readline.parse_and_bind() silently ignored on PyPy

findings.title: print(flush=True) may not flush immediately on PyPy
findings.description: print(flush=True) is called. On CPython this immediately flushes the output buffer. On PyPy, buffering behaviour differs — the flush may be delayed when writing to pipes or redirected stdout, causing output to appear out of order or be lost if the process crashes.
findings.suggestion: For critical output that must appear immediately on PyPy, use sys.stdout.flush() explicitly after print(), or set PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 in the environment before running on PyPy.

findings.title: id() values not stable across GC cycles on PyPy
findings.description: id() returns the memory address on CPython — stable for the object's lifetime. On PyPy, the GC may move objects in memory, so id() can return different values for the same object across GC cycles. Using id() for caching, hashing, or identity tracking may silently produce wrong results on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: Use object identity with 'is' instead of comparing id() values. For caching, use weakref or dedicated identity maps rather than id()-based keys.

findings.title: File write without explicit flush may lose data on PyPy
findings.description: A file is opened for writing. On PyPy, file buffering behaviour differs from CPython — data may not be flushed to disk even after close() due to GC timing differences. Without explicit flush() or a context manager, writes can be silently lost on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: Always use 'with open(...) as f:' to guarantee flushing and closing. If not using a context manager, call f.flush() explicitly before f.close().

findings.title: open() without encoding= uses platform-dependent encoding before 3.15

findings.title: __debug__ is always True on PyPy — -O flag has no effect

findings.title: id() values not stable across GC cycles on PyPy
findings.description: id() returns the memory address on CPython — stable for the object's lifetime. On PyPy, the GC may move objects in memory, so id() can return different values for the same object across GC cycles. findings.suggestion: Use object identity with 'is' instead of comparing id() values. For caching, use weakref or dedicated identity maps rather than id()-based keys.

findings.title: Relying on __del__ for resource cleanup breaks on PyPy

Before Python 3.15, the default encoding is the platform locale — UTF-8 on Linux/Mac but often CP1252 or Latin-1 on Windows. findings.title: Generator cleanup timing differs on PyPy

findings.title: id() values not stable across GC cycles on PyPy
findings.description: id() returns the memory address on CPython — stable for the object's lifetime. On PyPy, the GC may move objects in memory, so id() can return different values for the same object across GC cycles. Using id() for caching, hashing, or identity tracking may silently produce wrong results on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: Use object identity with 'is' instead of comparing id() values. For caching, use weakref or dedicated identity maps rather than id()-based keys.

findings.title: Unsynchronized module-level mutable state may be unsafe in free-threaded Python
findings.description: Module-level mutable variable '_caches' is mutated from runtime function code without recognizable synchronization. In a CPython free-threaded build, code that relies on the GIL to coordinate compound or unsynchronized access to shared state can behave differently.

findings.title: Relying on __del__ for resource cleanup breaks on PyPy
findings.description: __del__ calls 'close()' for resource cleanup. On CPython, __del__ is called immediately when the object goes out of scope (reference counting). On PyPy, the GC is non-reference-counting — __del__ may be called much later or not at all, silently leaking file handles, sockets, or locks.
findings.suggestion: Use context managers (with statement) or try/finally blocks for guaranteed cleanup. Never rely on __del__ for correctness.

findings.title: File write without explicit flush may lose data on PyPy
findings.description: A file is opened for writing. On PyPy, file buffering behaviour differs from CPython — data may not be flushed to disk even after close() due to GC timing differences. Without explicit flush() or a context manager, writes can be silently lost on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: Always use 'with open(...) as f:' to guarantee flushing and closing. If not using a context manager, call f.flush() explicitly before f.close().

findings.title: Exceptions in __del__ appear at unpredictable times on PyPy
findings.description: __del__ contains code that may raise exceptions. On CPython, exceptions in __del__ produce a warning to stderr immediately when the object is collected. On PyPy, the warning appears at an unpredictable time — possibly long after the object was collected — making debugging very difficult.
findings.suggestion: Wrap all __del__ body in try/except to prevent exceptions from escaping: try: self.cleanup() except Exception: pass. Better: use context managers instead of __del__.

findings.title: __slots__ may not prevent __dict__ on Python < 3.10
findings.description: Class 'WeakMethod' defines __slots__ but inherits from a non-trivial base class. findings.suggestion: Verify that all ancestor classes also define __slots__ if you need to prevent __dict__ creation. Use __slots__ = () on base classes that should not have instance dictionaries.

findings.title: id() values not stable across GC cycles on PyPy
findings.description: id() returns the memory address on CPython — stable for the object's lifetime. On PyPy, the GC may move objects in memory, so id() can return different values for the same object across GC cycles. Using id() for caching, hashing, or identity tracking may silently produce wrong results on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: Use object identity with 'is' instead of comparing id() values. For caching, use weakref or dedicated identity maps rather than id()-based keys.

findings.title: open() without encoding= uses platform-dependent encoding before 3.15
findings.description: open() is called in text mode without an explicit encoding= argument. Before Python 3.15, the default encoding is the platform locale — UTF-8 on Linux/Mac but often CP1252 or Latin-1 on Windows. This silently causes encoding errors or data corruption when code runs on different platforms. Python 3.15 (PEP 686) makes UTF-8 the universal default.
findings.suggestion: Always specify encoding explicitly: open(file, encoding='utf-8') This works correctly on all Python versions and platforms.

findings.title: File write without explicit flush may lose data on PyPy

findings.suggestion: Always use 'with open(...) as f:' to guarantee flushing and closing. If not using a context manager, call f.flush() explicitly before f.close().

findings.title: __slots__ may not prevent __dict__ on Python < 3.10
findings.description: Class 'Coroutine' defines __slots__ but inherits from a non-trivial base class. If any ancestor class has __dict__, __slots__ will NOT prevent __dict__ creation on the subclass. This behaviour is consistent across versions but commonly misunderstood — and Python 3.10 added clearer documentation and warnings around this pattern.
findings.suggestion: Verify that all ancestor classes also define __slots__ if you need to prevent __dict__ creation. Use __slots__ = () on base classes that should not have instance dictionaries.

findings.title: Instance __dict__ ordering not guaranteed on PyPy
findings.description: Accessing __dict__ on an instance. In CPython 3.7+, instance dictionaries are insertion-ordered. In PyPy, instance dicts use hidden classes for performance — if __init__ adds attributes in different orders across calls, dict order is not guaranteed to match CPython's.
findings.suggestion: Do not rely on instance __dict__ ordering. If you need ordered attributes, define them explicitly in __init__ in a consistent order, or use __slots__ to make the layout fixed.

findings.title: annotationlib requires Python 3.14+
findings.description: annotationlib was added in Python 3.14 (PEP 749). It provides tools for introspecting deferred annotations introduced by PEP 649. Importing it on Python 3.13 or below raises ModuleNotFoundError.
findings.suggestion: Guard with: if sys.version_info >= (3, 14): import annotationlib For 3.13 compatibility, use typing.get_type_hints() for annotation introspection instead.

findings.title: typing.Self requires Python 3.11+
findings.description: typing.Self was added in Python 3.11 (PEP 673). Importing it on Python 3.10 or below raises ImportError at runtime.
findings.suggestion: Guard with: if sys.version_info >= (3, 11): from typing import Self else: from typing_extensions import Self

findings.title: Instance __dict__ ordering not guaranteed on PyPy
findings.description: Accessing __dict__ on an instance. In CPython 3.7+, instance dictionaries are insertion-ordered. In PyPy, instance dicts use hidden classes for performance — if __init__ adds attributes in different orders across calls, dict order is not guaranteed to match CPython's.
findings.suggestion: Do not rely on instance __dict__ ordering. If you need ordered attributes, define them explicitly in __init__ in a consistent order, or use __slots__ to make the layout fixed.

findings.title: sys.flags values may differ between CPython and PyPy
findings.description: sys.flags.ignore_environment is accessed here. This flag may have different values or semantics on PyPy compared to CPython. In particular, hash_randomization is always 1 on PyPy regardless of PYTHONHASHSEED, and other flags may reflect PyPy-specific startup behaviour.
findings.suggestion: Do not rely on sys.flags values being identical between CPython and PyPy. Test explicitly on PyPy if your code behaviour depends on these flags.

findings.title: ctypes.util.find_library() unreliable on PyPy
findings.description: ctypes.util.find_library() is called here. On PyPy, this may return None or incorrect results even when the library exists.
findings.suggestion: Use cffi instead of ctypes on PyPy — it is fully supported and has reliable library discovery.

findings.title: File write without explicit flush may lose data on PyPy
findings.description: A file is opened for writing. On PyPy, file buffering behaviour differs from CPython — data may not be flushed to disk even after close() due to GC timing differences. Without explicit flush() or a context manager, writes can be silently lost on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: Always use 'with open(...) as f:' to guarantee flushing and closing. If not using a context manager, call f.flush() explicitly before f.close().

findings.title: __slots__ may not prevent __dict__ on Python < 3.10
findings.description: Class 'datetime' defines __slots__ but inherits from a non-trivial base class. If any ancestor class has __dict__, __slots__ will NOT prevent __dict__ creation on the subclass. This behaviour is consistent across versions but commonly misunderstood — and Python 3.10 added clearer documentation and warnings around this pattern.
findings.suggestion: Verify that all ancestor classes also define __slots__ if you need to prevent __dict__ creation. Use __slots__ = () on base classes that should not have instance dictionaries.

findings.title: str.removeprefix/removesuffix requires Python 3.9+
findings.description: str.removeprefix() was added in Python 3.9 (PEP 616). Calling it on Python 3.8 or below raises AttributeError at runtime.
findings.suggestion: For Python 3.8 compatibility: s[len(prefix):] if s.startswith(prefix) else s (for removeprefix) or s[:-len(suffix)] if s.endswith(suffix) else s (for removesuffix).

findings.title: hash() values may differ between CPython and PyPy
findings.description: hash() is called here. On CPython, hash(-1) returns -2 because -1 is reserved as an error indicator in C. PyPy matches this for integers, but hash values for certain custom objects or edge cases may differ between runtimes. Code that stores or compares hash values across sessions or runtimes may silently fail.
findings.suggestion: Never store hash values persistently or compare them across different Python runtimes. Hash values are implementation-specific and not guaranteed to be consistent between CPython and PyPy.

findings.title: Relying on __del__ for resource cleanup breaks on PyPy
findings.description: __del__ calls 'close()' for resource cleanup. On CPython, __del__ is called immediately when the object goes out of scope (reference counting). On PyPy, the GC is non-reference-counting — __del__ may be called much later or not at all, silently leaking file handles, sockets, or locks.
findings.suggestion: Use context managers (with statement) or try/finally blocks for guaranteed cleanup. Never rely on __del__ for correctness.

findings.title: Exceptions in __del__ appear at unpredictable times on PyPy
findings.description: __del__ contains code that may raise exceptions. On CPython, exceptions in __del__ produce a warning to stderr immediately when the object is collected. On PyPy, the warning appears at an unpredictable time — possibly long after the object was collected — making debugging very difficult.
findings.suggestion: Wrap all __del__ body in try/except to prevent exceptions from escaping: try: self.cleanup() except Exception: pass. Better: use context managers instead of __del__.

findings.title: id() values not stable across GC cycles on PyPy
findings.description: id() returns the memory address on CPython — stable for the object's lifetime. On PyPy, the GC may move objects in memory, so id() can return different values for the same object across GC cycles. Using id() for caching, hashing, or identity tracking may silently produce wrong results on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: Use object identity with 'is' instead of comparing id() values. For caching, use weakref or dedicated identity maps rather than id()-based keys.

findings.title: Socket not closed promptly on PyPy — GC timing
findings.description: A socket is created here. On CPython, sockets are closed immediately when they go out of scope (reference counting). On PyPy, sockets are closed by the GC which may run much later — you can silently exhaust the OS limit on open file descriptors in long-running servers without any error until the limit is hit.
findings.suggestion: Always use sockets as context managers: 'with socket.socket() as s:' to guarantee prompt closure on both CPython and PyPy.

findings.title: id() values not stable across GC cycles on PyPy
findings.description: id() returns the memory address on CPython — stable for the object's lifetime. On PyPy, the GC may move objects in memory, so id() can return different values for the same object across GC cycles. Using id() for caching, hashing, or identity tracking may silently produce wrong results on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: Use object identity with 'is' instead of comparing id() values. For caching, use weakref or dedicated identity maps rather than id()-based keys.

findings.title: Relying on __del__ for resource cleanup breaks on PyPy

findings.suggestion: Wrap all __del__ body in try/except to prevent exceptions from escaping: try: self.cleanup() except Exception: pass. Better: use context managers instead of __del__.

findings.title: hash() values may differ between CPython and PyPy
findings.description: hash() is called here. On CPython, hash(-1) returns -2 because -1 is reserved as an error indicator in C. PyPy matches this for integers, but hash values for certain custom objects or edge cases may differ between runtimes. Code that stores or compares hash values across sessions or runtimes may silently fail.
findings.suggestion: Never store hash values persistently or compare them across different Python runtimes. Hash values are implementation-specific and not guaranteed to be consistent between CPython and PyPy.

findings.title: ctypes.util.find_library() unreliable on PyPy

findings.title: __slots__ may not prevent __dict__ on Python < 3.10
findings.description: Class 'BigEndianStructure' defines __slots__ but inherits from a non-trivial base class. If any ancestor class has __dict__, __slots__ will NOT prevent __dict__ creation on the subclass. This behaviour is consistent across versions but commonly misunderstood — and Python 3.10 added clearer documentation and warnings around this pattern.
findings.suggestion: Verify that all ancestor classes also define __slots__ if you need to prevent __dict__ creation. Use __slots__ = () on base classes that should not have instance dictionaries.

findings.title: __slots__ memory savings differ on PyPy

findings.suggestion: __slots__ is still correct and beneficial on PyPy — just measure memory usage independently on each runtime rather than assuming CPython numbers apply.

findings.title: id() values not stable across GC cycles on PyPy
findings.description: id() returns the memory address on CPython — stable for the object's lifetime. On PyPy, the GC may move objects in memory, so id() can return different values for the same object across GC cycles. Using id() for caching, hashing, or identity tracking may silently produce wrong results on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: Use object identity with 'is' instead of comparing id() values. For caching, use weakref or dedicated identity maps rather than id()-based keys.

findings.title: locals() semantics changed in Python 3.13 (PEP 667)
findings.description: locals() is called here. Before Python 3.13, modifying the dict returned by locals() had undefined behaviour — changes sometimes affected local variables. In Python 3.13 (PEP 667), locals() returns a snapshot and modifying it never affects actual local variables. Code relying on locals() mutation will silently break.
findings.suggestion: Do not modify the dict returned by locals(). Use explicit variable assignment instead. If you need dynamic variable access, use a regular dict.

findings.title: open() without encoding= uses platform-dependent encoding before 3.15
findings.description: open() is called in text mode without an explicit encoding= argument. Before Python 3.15, the default encoding is the platform locale — UTF-8 on Linux/Mac but often CP1252 or Latin-1 on Windows. This silently causes encoding errors or data corruption when code runs on different platforms. Python 3.15 (PEP 686) makes UTF-8 the universal default.
findings.suggestion: Always specify encoding explicitly: open(file, encoding='utf-8') This works correctly on all Python versions and platforms.

findings.title: Unsynchronized module-level mutable state may be unsafe in free-threaded Python
findings.description: Module-level mutable variable '_c_functype_cache' is mutated from runtime function code without recognizable synchronization. In a CPython free-threaded build, code that relies on the GIL to coordinate compound or unsynchronized access to shared state can behave differently.
findings.suggestion: If this state is shared across threads, protect compound mutations and read-modify-write sequences with a lock, or use an appropriate thread-safe abstraction. Individual built-in list/dict/set operations should not be treated as a blanket guarantee of thread safety.

findings.title: Instance __dict__ ordering not guaranteed on PyPy
findings.description: Accessing __dict__ on an instance. In CPython 3.7+, instance dictionaries are insertion-ordered. In PyPy, instance dicts use hidden classes for performance — if __init__ adds attributes in different orders across calls, dict order is not guaranteed to match CPython's.
findings.suggestion: Do not rely on instance __dict__ ordering. If you need ordered attributes, define them explicitly in __init__ in a consistent order, or use __slots__ to make the layout fixed.

findings.title: Generator cleanup timing differs on PyPy
findings.description: Generator '__iter__' yields inside a try/with block. On CPython, if a generator is abandoned mid-execution, the finally/cleanup runs promptly via reference counting. On PyPy, the generator is GC'd later — finally blocks and context manager __exit__ may run much later or at unpredictable times, silently leaking resources.

findings.title: File write without explicit flush may lose data on PyPy

findings.title: open() without encoding= uses platform-dependent encoding before 3.15

findings.title: sys.setrecursionlimit() behaviour differs on PyPy
findings.description: sys.setrecursionlimit(n) on CPython sets the exact maximum recursion depth to n. On PyPy, it sets the usable stack space to n * 768 bytes — the actual number of recursive calls allowed depends on frame size and is approximately n/5 on most platforms. findings.suggestion: If you need deep recursion on PyPy, set the limit significantly higher than on CPython, or convert the recursion to an explicit stack-based iteration.

findings.title: open() without encoding= uses platform-dependent encoding before 3.15
findings.description: open() is called in text mode without an explicit encoding= argument. Before Python 3.15, the default encoding is the platform locale — UTF-8 on Linux/Mac but often CP1252 or Latin-1 on Windows. This silently causes encoding errors or data corruption when code runs on different platforms. Python 3.15 (PEP 686) makes UTF-8 the universal default.
findings.suggestion: Always specify encoding explicitly: open(file, encoding='utf-8') This works correctly on all Python versions and platforms.

findings.title: Instance __dict__ ordering not guaranteed on PyPy
findings.description: Accessing __dict__ on an instance. In CPython 3.7+, instance dictionaries are insertion-ordered. In PyPy, instance dicts use hidden classes for performance — if __init__ adds attributes in different orders across calls, dict order is not guaranteed to match CPython's.
findings.suggestion: Do not rely on instance __dict__ ordering. If you need ordered attributes, define them explicitly in __init__ in a consistent order, or use __slots__ to make the layout fixed.

findings.title: Instance __dict__ ordering not guaranteed on PyPy

findings.suggestion: Do not rely on instance __dict__ ordering. If you need ordered attributes, define them explicitly in __init__ in a consistent order, or use __slots__ to make the layout fixed.

findings.title: Overriding built-in methods may behave differently on PyPy
findings.description: Class 'S' subclasses 'str' and overrides '__len__'. On CPython, internal C-level calls to built-in methods may bypass Python overrides. On PyPy, the same calls may go through the Python override. This can cause silent behaviour differences between runtimes.
findings.suggestion: Test the overridden method explicitly on both CPython and PyPy. Consider using composition instead of inheritance from built-in types.

findings.title: sys.setrecursionlimit() behaviour differs on PyPy
findings.description: sys.setrecursionlimit(n) on CPython sets the exact maximum recursion depth to n. On PyPy, it sets the usable stack space to n * 768 bytes — the actual number of recursive calls allowed depends on frame size and is approximately n/5 on most platforms. Code that sets a specific recursion limit may behave differently on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: If you need deep recursion on PyPy, set the limit significantly higher than on CPython, or convert the recursion to an explicit stack-based iteration.

findings.title: Generator cleanup timing differs on PyPy
findings.description: Generator 'test_very_long_wrapped_line' yields inside a try/with block. On CPython, if a generator is abandoned mid-execution, the finally/cleanup runs promptly via reference counting. On PyPy, the generator is GC'd later — finally blocks and context manager __exit__ may run much later or at unpredictable times, silently leaking resources.
findings.suggestion: Always fully exhaust generators or use explicit close(): gen.close(). Use try/finally in the caller to guarantee cleanup rather than relying on generator GC.

findings.title: open() without encoding= uses platform-dependent encoding before 3.15
findings.description: open() is called in text mode without an explicit encoding= argument. Before Python 3.15, the default encoding is the platform locale — UTF-8 on Linux/Mac but often CP1252 or Latin-1 on Windows. This silently causes encoding errors or data corruption when code runs on different platforms. Python 3.15 (PEP 686) makes UTF-8 the universal default.
findings.suggestion: Always specify encoding explicitly: open(file, encoding='utf-8') This works correctly on all Python versions and platforms.

findings.title: hash() values may differ between CPython and PyPy

Code that stores or compares hash values across sessions or runtimes may silently fail.

PyPy matches this for integers, but hash values for certain custom objects or edge cases may differ between runtimes. Code that stores or compares hash values across sessions or runtimes may silently fail.
findings.suggestion: Never store hash values persistently or compare them across different Python runtimes. Hash values are implementation-specific and not guaranteed to be consistent between CPython and PyPy.

findings.title: datetime.utcnow() deprecated since Python 3.12
findings.description: datetime.datetime.utcnow() is deprecated since Python 3.12. It returns a naive datetime object with no timezone information, making it dangerously easy to confuse with local time. It will be removed in a future Python version.
findings.suggestion: Use datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc) which returns a timezone-aware UTC datetime. Or with Python 3.11+: datetime.datetime.now(datetime.UTC)

findings.title: datetime.utcfromtimestamp() deprecated since Python 3.12
findings.description: datetime.datetime.utcfromtimestamp() is deprecated since Python 3.12. It returns a naive datetime with no timezone information. This is a common source of timezone bugs in logging, data pipelines, and APIs.
findings.suggestion: Use datetime.datetime.fromtimestamp(ts, datetime.timezone.utc) which returns a timezone-aware UTC datetime. Works on all Python 3 versions.

findings.title: decimal module uses different backend on PyPy
findings.description: The decimal module is imported. On CPython, decimal uses a fast C implementation. On PyPy, it uses a pure Python/RPython implementation which is slower and may have subtle differences in rounding behaviour and context handling in edge cases.
findings.suggestion: Test decimal-heavy code on PyPy explicitly. For high-precision financial calculations, verify rounding behaviour matches expectations on both CPython and PyPy with your specific data.

findings.title: __slots__ memory savings differ on PyPy
findings.description: Class 'PicklableFixedOffsetWithSlots' defines __slots__. On CPython, __slots__ prevents __dict__ creation and gives predictable memory savings. On PyPy, object layout uses hidden classes — __slots__ works correctly but memory savings differ from CPython. Do not rely on specific memory numbers from CPython when running on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: __slots__ is still correct and beneficial on PyPy — just measure memory usage independently on each runtime rather than assuming CPython numbers apply.

findings.title: open() without encoding= uses platform-dependent encoding before 3.15
findings.description: open() is called in text mode without an explicit encoding= argument. Before Python 3.15, the default encoding is the platform locale — UTF-8 on Linux/Mac but often CP1252 or Latin-1 on Windows. This silently causes encoding errors or data corruption when code runs on different platforms. Python 3.15 (PEP 686) makes UTF-8 the universal default.
findings.suggestion: Always specify encoding explicitly: open(file, encoding='utf-8') This works correctly on all Python versions and platforms.

findings.title: pickle default protocol changed to 5 in Python 3.14
findings.description: pickle.dumps() is called without an explicit protocol= argument. Python 3.14 changed the default pickle protocol from 4 to 5. Data pickled with the default on 3.14+ cannot be unpickled by Python 3.7 or below. This silently causes 'ValueError: unsupported pickle protocol: 5' on older Python versions.
findings.suggestion: Specify the protocol explicitly for cross-version compatibility: pickle.dumps(obj, protocol=4) for Python 3.4+ compatibility, or protocol=2 for maximum compatibility. Use pickle.HIGHEST_PROTOCOL only when cross-version compatibility is not required.

findings.title: os.fork() may not work correctly on all PyPy platforms
findings.description: os.fork() is called here. On PyPy, forking a process with active JIT-compiled code can cause issues — the JIT state may not be properly reset in the child process, leading to silent crashes or incorrect behaviour. PyPy also does not support os.fork() on all platforms it runs on.
findings.suggestion: Use multiprocessing with spawn or forkserver start methods instead of os.fork() directly. These are safer on both CPython and PyPy.

findings.title: id() values not stable across GC cycles on PyPy
findings.description: id() returns the memory address on CPython — stable for the object's lifetime. On PyPy, the GC may move objects in memory, so id() can return different values for the same object across GC cycles. Using id() for caching, hashing, or identity tracking may silently produce wrong results on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: Use object identity with 'is' instead of comparing id() values. For caching, use weakref or dedicated identity maps rather than id()-based keys.

findings.title: ExceptionGroup requires Python 3.11+
findings.description: ExceptionGroup was introduced in Python 3.11 (PEP 654). On Python 3.10 and below, using it raises NameError at runtime — it does not exist as a built-in.
findings.suggestion: Guard with: if sys.version_info >= (3, 11): or use the exceptiongroup backport package (pip install exceptiongroup) for 3.10 compatibility.

findings.title: gc.collect() behaviour differs on PyPy
findings.description: gc.collect() on CPython triggers a full cyclic garbage collection and returns the number of objects collected. On PyPy, gc.collect() exists but uses a different GC algorithm — the return value has different semantics and cleanup is not guaranteed to be immediate. Code relying on gc.collect() for deterministic resource release will behave differently on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: Do not rely on gc.collect() for deterministic cleanup. Use context managers and explicit close() calls instead. If testing memory behaviour, run tests on both runtimes.

findings.title: multiprocessing default start method changing in Python 3.14
findings.description: The default multiprocessing start method on Linux/BSD/POSIX is 'fork' in Python <= 3.13. In Python 3.14 it will change to a safer method. Code relying on fork semantics (shared memory, inherited file descriptors) may silently break.
findings.suggestion: Explicitly set the start method: multiprocessing.set_start_method('fork') or use multiprocessing.get_context('fork') to make the behaviour explicit and version-safe.

findings.title: Deleting module/class attributes is significantly slower on PyPy
findings.description: Attribute 'errors' is being deleted. On PyPy, module and class dictionaries are optimised under the assumption that deleting attributes is rare. Frequent attribute deletion is significantly slower on PyPy than on CPython and will silently degrade performance in hot paths.
findings.suggestion: Avoid frequent attribute deletion in hot code paths. Set attributes to None instead of deleting them, or restructure code to avoid deletion entirely.

findings.title: __slots__ may not prevent __dict__ on Python < 3.10
findings.description: Class 'WithSlotsSubclass' defines __slots__ but inherits from a non-trivial base class. If any ancestor class has __dict__, __slots__ will NOT prevent __dict__ creation on the subclass. This behaviour is consistent across versions but commonly misunderstood — and Python 3.10 added clearer documentation and warnings around this pattern.
findings.suggestion: Verify that all ancestor classes also define __slots__ if you need to prevent __dict__ creation. Use __slots__ = () on base classes that should not have instance dictionaries.

findings.title: Instance __dict__ ordering not guaranteed on PyPy
findings.description: Accessing __dict__ on an instance. In CPython 3.7+, instance dictionaries are insertion-ordered. In PyPy, instance dicts use hidden classes for performance — if __init__ adds attributes in different orders across calls, dict order is not guaranteed to match CPython's.
findings.suggestion: Do not rely on instance __dict__ ordering. If you need ordered attributes, define them explicitly in __init__ in a consistent order, or use __slots__ to make the layout fixed.

findings.title: weakref.proxy() behaviour differs on PyPy
findings.description: weakref.proxy() can raise ReferenceError at unpredictable points on PyPy due to its tracing GC — not just when the proxied object is accessed after death as on CPython. Code must catch ReferenceError at every access point, not just at the final dereference.
findings.suggestion: Use weakref.ref() instead of weakref.proxy() — call ref() to get the object and check for None explicitly. This is safer on both CPython and PyPy.

findings.title: File write without explicit flush may lose data on PyPy
findings.description: A file is opened for writing. On PyPy, file buffering behaviour differs from CPython — data may not be flushed to disk even after close() due to GC timing differences. Without explicit flush() or a context manager, writes can be silently lost on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: Always use 'with open(...) as f:' to guarantee flushing and closing. If not using a context manager, call f.flush() explicitly before f.close().

findings.title: open() without encoding= uses platform-dependent encoding before 3.15
findings.description: open() is called in text mode without an explicit encoding= argument. Before Python 3.15, the default encoding is the platform locale — UTF-8 on Linux/Mac but often CP1252 or Latin-1 on Windows. This silently causes encoding errors or data corruption when code runs on different platforms. Python 3.15 (PEP 686) makes UTF-8 the universal default.
findings.suggestion: Always specify encoding explicitly: open(file, encoding='utf-8') This works correctly on all Python versions and platforms.

findings.title: ctypes usage may silently fail on PyPy
findings.description: ctypes.WinDLL is used here. PyPy's ctypes implementation is incomplete — pointer arithmetic, callbacks, and bit-field structures may silently produce wrong results or segfault on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: Test explicitly on PyPy if ctypes is required. Consider cffi as a cross-runtime alternative — fully supported on both CPython and PyPy.

findings.title: subprocess.PIPE buffering may cause deadlocks on PyPy
findings.description: Popen is called with stdout=PIPE. On PyPy, GC timing differences can cause subprocess pipe communication to deadlock or lose data silently — especially when both stdin and stdout use PIPE and the buffers fill up before communicate() is called.
findings.suggestion: Always use communicate() instead of read()/write() directly on pipes. communicate() handles buffering correctly on both CPython and PyPy.

findings.title: id() values not stable across GC cycles on PyPy
findings.description: id() returns the memory address on CPython — stable for the object's lifetime. On PyPy, the GC may move objects in memory, so id() can return different values for the same object across GC cycles. Using id() for caching, hashing, or identity tracking may silently produce wrong results on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: Use object identity with 'is' instead of comparing id() values. For caching, use weakref or dedicated identity maps rather than id()-based keys.

findings.title: Generator cleanup timing differs on PyPy
findings.description: Generator 'test_join' yields inside a try/with block. On CPython, if a generator is abandoned mid-execution, the finally/cleanup runs promptly via reference counting. findings.title: dict | merge operator requires Python 3.9+
findings.description: The | operator for dict merging was added in Python 3.9 (PEP 584). Using it on Python 3.8 or below raises TypeError at runtime.
findings.suggestion: For Python 3.8 compatibility use: {**d1, **d2} for merging, or d1.update(d2) for in-place update.

findings.title: string.templatelib requires Python 3.14+
findings.description: string.templatelib was added in Python 3.14 (PEP 750). It provides support for t-string template literals which create Template objects instead of plain strings. Importing it on Python 3.13 or below raises ModuleNotFoundError at runtime.
findings.suggestion: Guard with: if sys.version_info >= (3, 14): from string.templatelib import Template, Interpolation T-strings are not backportable — use f-strings or string.Template for Python 3.13 compatibility.

findings.title: annotationlib requires Python 3.14+
findings.description: annotationlib was added in Python 3.14 (PEP 749). It provides tools for introspecting deferred annotations introduced by PEP 649. Importing it on Python 3.13 or below raises ModuleNotFoundError.
findings.suggestion: Guard with: if sys.version_info >= (3, 14): import annotationlib For 3.13 compatibility, use typing.get_type_hints() for annotation introspection instead.

findings.title: Overriding built-in methods may behave differently on PyPy
findings.description: Class 'CustomStr' subclasses 'str' and overrides '__len__'. On CPython, internal C-level calls to built-in methods may bypass Python overrides. On PyPy, the same calls may go through the Python override. This can cause silent behaviour differences between runtimes.
findings.suggestion: Test the overridden method explicitly on both CPython and PyPy. Consider using composition instead of inheritance from built-in types.

findings.title: File write without explicit flush may lose data on PyPy
findings.description: A file is opened for writing. On PyPy, file buffering behaviour differs from CPython — data may not be flushed to disk even after close() due to GC timing differences. Without explicit flush() or a context manager, writes can be silently lost on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: Always use 'with open(...) as f:' to guarantee flushing and closing. If not using a context manager, call f.flush() explicitly before f.close().

findings.title: Instance __dict__ ordering not guaranteed on PyPy
findings.description: Accessing __dict__ on an instance. In CPython 3.7+, instance dictionaries are insertion-ordered. In PyPy, instance dicts use hidden classes for performance — if __init__ adds attributes in different orders across calls, dict order is not guaranteed to match CPython's.
findings.suggestion: Do not rely on instance __dict__ ordering. If you need ordered attributes, define them explicitly in __init__ in a consistent order, or use __slots__ to make the layout fixed.

findings.title: __slots__ may not prevent __dict__ on Python < 3.10
findings.description: Class 'ExaggeratingArray' defines __slots__ but inherits from a non-trivial base class. If any ancestor class has __dict__, __slots__ will NOT prevent __dict__ creation on the subclass. This behaviour is consistent across versions but commonly misunderstood — and Python 3.10 added clearer documentation and warnings around this pattern.
findings.suggestion: Verify that all ancestor classes also define __slots__ if you need to prevent __dict__ creation. Use __slots__ = () on base classes that should not have instance dictionaries.

findings.title: sys.getrefcount() is meaningless on PyPy
findings.description: sys.getrefcount() relies on CPython's reference counting GC. PyPy uses a tracing GC with no reference counting — sys.getrefcount() always returns a dummy value on PyPy. Any logic based on this value will silently produce wrong results on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: Do not use sys.getrefcount() for correctness logic. If debugging memory, use gc.get_referrers() instead which works on both runtimes.

findings.title: weakref.proxy() behaviour differs on PyPy
findings.description: weakref.proxy() can raise ReferenceError at unpredictable points on PyPy due to its tracing GC — not just when the proxied object is accessed after death as on CPython. Code must catch ReferenceError at every access point, not just at the final dereference.
findings.suggestion: Use weakref.ref() instead of weakref.proxy() — call ref() to get the object and check for None explicitly. This is safer on both CPython and PyPy.

findings.title: id() values not stable across GC cycles on PyPy
findings.description: id() returns the memory address on CPython — stable for the object's lifetime. On PyPy, the GC may move objects in memory, so id() can return different values for the same object across GC cycles. Using id() for caching, hashing, or identity tracking may silently produce wrong results on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: Use object identity with 'is' instead of comparing id() values. For caching, use weakref or dedicated identity maps rather than id()-based keys.

findings.title: gc.collect() behaviour differs on PyPy
findings.description: gc.collect() on CPython triggers a full cyclic garbage collection and returns the number of objects collected. On PyPy, gc.collect() exists but uses a different GC algorithm — the return value has different semantics and cleanup is not guaranteed to be immediate. Code relying on gc.collect() for deterministic resource release will behave differently on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: Do not rely on gc.collect() for deterministic cleanup. Use context managers and explicit close() calls instead. If testing memory behaviour, run tests on both runtimes.

findings.title: float('nan') identity differs between CPython and PyPy
findings.description: float('nan') creates a new object each time on CPython — so float('nan') is float('nan') is False and a set can contain multiple NaN values. On PyPy, there is only one NaN object per bit pattern — float('nan') is float('nan') is True, and a set cannot contain multiple NaN values. This causes silent behaviour differences in set operations.
findings.suggestion: Use math.isnan() to check for NaN rather than identity comparisons. Do not rely on multiple NaN values in a set — use filtering instead.

findings.title: __slots__ memory savings differ on PyPy
findings.description: Class 'ExaggeratingArray' defines __slots__. On CPython, __slots__ prevents __dict__ creation and gives predictable memory savings. On PyPy, object layout uses hidden classes — __slots__ works correctly but memory savings differ from CPython. Do not rely on specific memory numbers from CPython when running on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: __slots__ is still correct and beneficial on PyPy — just measure memory usage independently on each runtime rather than assuming CPython numbers apply.

findings.title: Generator cleanup timing differs on PyPy
findings.description: Generator 'test_async_gen_exception_07' yields inside a try/with block. On CPython, if a generator is abandoned mid-execution, the finally/cleanup runs promptly via reference counting. On PyPy, the generator is GC'd later — finally blocks and context manager __exit__ may run much later or at unpredictable times, silently leaking resources.
findings.suggestion: Always fully exhaust generators or use explicit close(): gen.close(). Use try/finally in the caller to guarantee cleanup rather than relying on generator GC.

findings.title: aiter() and anext() builtins require Python 3.10+
findings.description: aiter() was added as a builtin in Python 3.10. Calling it on Python 3.9 or below raises NameError at runtime — it does not exist as a builtin.
findings.suggestion: Guard with: if sys.version_info >= (3, 10): use aiter() or implement the async iteration manually for 3.9.

findings.title: Exception variable cleanup timing differs on PyPy
findings.description: Exception variable 'ex' is used after the except handler exits. CPython explicitly clears exception variables at the end of an except handler to break reference cycles. Depending on exception-variable lifetime can therefore interact differently with PyPy's garbage collector.
findings.suggestion: If 'ex' must remain available after the except block, explicitly copy it to another variable inside the handler, for example: saved_exc = ex.

findings.title: subprocess.PIPE buffering may cause deadlocks on PyPy
findings.description: Popen is called with stdout=PIPE. On PyPy, GC timing differences can cause subprocess pipe communication to deadlock or lose data silently — especially when both stdin and stdout use PIPE and the buffers fill up before communicate() is called.
findings.suggestion: Always use communicate() instead of read()/write() directly on pipes. communicate() handles buffering correctly on both CPython and PyPy.

findings.title: dict | merge operator requires Python 3.9+
findings.description: The |= operator for dict update was added in Python 3.9 (PEP 584). Using it on Python 3.8 or below raises TypeError at runtime.
findings.suggestion: For Python 3.8 compatibility use: d1.update(d2) instead of d1 |= d2.

findings.title: File write without explicit flush may lose data on PyPy
findings.description: A file is opened for writing. On PyPy, file buffering behaviour differs from CPython — data may not be flushed to disk even after close() due to GC timing differences. Without explicit flush() or a context manager, writes can be silently lost on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: Always use 'with open(...) as f:' to guarantee flushing and closing. If not using a context manager, call f.flush() explicitly before f.close().

findings.title: gc.collect() behaviour differs on PyPy
findings.description: gc.collect() on CPython triggers a full cyclic garbage collection and returns the number of objects collected. On PyPy, gc.collect() exists but uses a different GC algorithm — the return value has different semantics and cleanup is not guaranteed to be immediate. Code relying on gc.collect() for deterministic resource release will behave differently on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: Do not rely on gc.collect() for deterministic cleanup. Use context managers and explicit close() calls instead. If testing memory behaviour, run tests on both runtimes.

findings.title: Instance __dict__ ordering not guaranteed on PyPy
findings.description: Accessing __dict__ on an instance. In CPython 3.7+, instance dictionaries are insertion-ordered. In PyPy, instance dicts use hidden classes for performance — if __init__ adds attributes in different orders across calls, dict order is not guaranteed to match CPython's.
findings.suggestion: Do not rely on instance __dict__ ordering. If you need ordered attributes, define them explicitly in __init__ in a consistent order, or use __slots__ to make the layout fixed.

findings.title: String concatenation in loop is O(n²) on PyPy
findings.description: String variable 'info' is concatenated with += inside a loop. Repeated string concatenation can have different performance characteristics on PyPy and may become O(n²) for large inputs.
findings.suggestion: Use a list and join at the end: parts = []; parts.append(s); result = ''.join(parts). This avoids repeated string concatenation.

findings.title: Generator cleanup timing differs on PyPy
findings.description: Generator 'run_test' yields inside a try/with block. On CPython, if a generator is abandoned mid-execution, the finally/cleanup runs promptly via reference counting. On PyPy, the generator is GC'd later — finally blocks and context manager __exit__ may run much later or at unpredictable times, silently leaking resources.
findings.suggestion: Always fully exhaust generators or use explicit close(): gen.close(). Use try/finally in the caller to guarantee cleanup rather than relying on generator GC.

findings.title: sys.settrace() disables JIT and is unreliable on PyPy
findings.description: sys.settrace() is called. On CPython, this installs a tracing function for debugging and profiling. On PyPy, sys.settrace() disables the JIT compiler entirely — causing 10-100x performance degradation — and some trace events may not fire correctly. Coverage tools and debuggers using settrace will silently give incomplete results on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: For profiling on PyPy, use vmprof instead of settrace-based profilers. For coverage, use coverage.py with PyPy-specific configuration. Avoid settrace in production code on PyPy.

findings.title: hash() values may differ between CPython and PyPy
findings.description: hash() is called here. On CPython, hash(-1) returns -2 because -1 is reserved as an error indicator in C. PyPy matches this for integers, but hash values for certain custom objects or edge cases may differ between runtimes. Code that stores or compares hash values across sessions or runtimes may silently fail.
findings.suggestion: Never store hash values persistently or compare them across different Python runtimes. Hash values are implementation-specific and not guaranteed to be consistent between CPython and PyPy.

findings.title: dict(**kwargs) requires string keys on PyPy and Python 3
findings.description: A non-string key (1) is used in a dict passed as **kwargs. On PyPy and CPython 3.x, this raises TypeError. Only string keys are allowed in **kwargs.
findings.suggestion: Ensure all keys in **kwargs dicts are strings. Use positional arguments or a regular dict argument instead of **unpacking with non-string keys.

findings.title: __slots__ memory savings differ on PyPy
findings.description: Class 'Rat' defines __slots__. On CPython, __slots__ prevents __dict__ creation and gives predictable memory savings. On PyPy, object layout uses hidden classes — __slots__ works correctly but memory savings differ from CPython. Do not rely on specific memory numbers from CPython when running on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: __slots__ is still correct and beneficial on PyPy — just measure memory usage independently on each runtime rather than assuming CPython numbers apply.

findings.title: String concatenation in loop is O(n²) on PyPy
findings.description: String variable 'xfmt' is concatenated with += inside a loop. Repeated string concatenation can have different performance characteristics on PyPy and may become O(n²) for large inputs.
findings.suggestion: Use a list and join at the end: parts = []; parts.append(s); result = ''.join(parts). This avoids repeated string concatenation.

findings.title: Generator cleanup timing differs on PyPy
findings.description: Generator 'assert_out_of_bounds_error' yields inside a try/with block. On CPython, if a generator is abandoned mid-execution, the finally/cleanup runs promptly via reference counting. On PyPy, the generator is GC'd later — finally blocks and context manager __exit__ may run much later or at unpredictable times, silently leaking resources.
findings.suggestion: Always fully exhaust generators or use explicit close(): gen.close(). Use try/finally in the caller to guarantee cleanup rather than relying on generator GC.

findings.title: float('nan') identity differs between CPython and PyPy
findings.description: float('nan') creates a new object each time on CPython — so float('nan') is float('nan') is False and a set can contain multiple NaN values. On PyPy, there is only one NaN object per bit pattern — float('nan') is float('nan') is True, and a set cannot contain multiple NaN values. This causes silent behaviour differences in set operations.
findings.suggestion: Use math.isnan() to check for NaN rather than identity comparisons. Do not rely on multiple NaN values in a set — use filtering instead.

findings.title: locals() semantics changed in Python 3.13 (PEP 667)
findings.description: locals() is called here. Before Python 3.13, modifying the dict returned by locals() had undefined behaviour — changes sometimes affected local variables. In Python 3.13 (PEP 667), locals() returns a snapshot and modifying it never affects actual local variables. Code relying on locals() mutation will silently break.
findings.suggestion: Do not modify the dict returned by locals(). Use explicit variable assignment instead. If you need dynamic variable access, use a regular dict.

findings.title: str.removeprefix/removesuffix requires Python 3.9+
findings.description: str.removeprefix() was added in Python 3.9 (PEP 616). Calling it on Python 3.8 or below raises AttributeError at runtime.
findings.suggestion: For Python 3.8 compatibility: s[len(prefix):] if s.startswith(prefix) else s (for removeprefix) or s[:-len(suffix)] if s.endswith(suffix) else s (for removesuffix).

findings.title: hash() values may differ between CPython and PyPy
findings.description: hash() is called here. On CPython, hash(-1) returns -2 because -1 is reserved as an error indicator in C. PyPy matches this for integers, but hash values for certain custom objects or edge cases may differ between runtimes. Code that stores or compares hash values across sessions or runtimes may silently fail.
findings.suggestion: Never store hash values persistently or compare them across different Python runtimes. Hash values are implementation-specific and not guaranteed to be consistent between CPython and PyPy.

findings.title: sys.getrefcount() is meaningless on PyPy
findings.description: sys.getrefcount() relies on CPython's reference counting GC. PyPy uses a tracing GC with no reference counting — sys.getrefcount() always returns a dummy value on PyPy. Any logic based on this value will silently produce wrong results on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: Do not use sys.getrefcount() for correctness logic. If debugging memory, use gc.get_referrers() instead which works on both runtimes.

findings.title: File write without explicit flush may lose data on PyPy
findings.description: A file is opened for writing. On PyPy, file buffering behaviour differs from CPython — data may not be flushed to disk even after close() due to GC timing differences. Without explicit flush() or a context manager, writes can be silently lost on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: Always use 'with open(...) as f:' to guarantee flushing and closing. If not using a context manager, call f.flush() explicitly before f.close().

findings.title: id() values not stable across GC cycles on PyPy
findings.description: id() returns the memory address on CPython — stable for the object's lifetime. On PyPy, the GC may move objects in memory, so id() can return different values for the same object across GC cycles. Using id() for caching, hashing, or identity tracking may silently produce wrong results on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: Use object identity with 'is' instead of comparing id() values. For caching, use weakref or dedicated identity maps rather than id()-based keys.

findings.title: gc.collect() behaviour differs on PyPy
findings.description: gc.collect() on CPython triggers a full cyclic garbage collection and returns the number of objects collected. On PyPy, gc.collect() exists but uses a different GC algorithm — the return value has different semantics and cleanup is not guaranteed to be immediate. Code relying on gc.collect() for deterministic resource release will behave differently on PyPy.
findings.suggestion: Do not rely on gc.collect() for deterministic cleanup. Use context managers and explicit close() calls instead. If testing memory behaviour, run tests on both runtimes.

findings.title: Overriding built-in methods may behave differently on PyPy
findings.description: Class 'D' subclasses 'dict' and overrides '__getitem__'. On CPython, internal C-level calls to built-in methods may bypass Python overrides. On PyPy, the same calls may go through the Python override. This can cause silent behaviour differences between runtimes.
findings.suggestion: Test the overridden method explicitly on both CPython and PyPy. Consider using composition instead of inheritance from built-in types.
